html:
The many non-Chinese peoples of China's southeast coast, known to Chinese writers as the Hundred Yue. The map shows them in 323 and 300 BCE along the coasts of what are now Fujian and Guangdong.

The Yue grew rice in wet fields, fished, built houses on stilts, tattooed their bodies and cut their hair short, all marks of difference to northern writers. In the north of their range stood the kingdom of Yue in Zhejiang, whose king Goujian famously crushed the rival state of Wu in 473 BCE. That kingdom was broken by Chu in the late 4th century BCE, during the Warring States period, and its ruling families scattered south.

From them came coastal kingdoms such as Minyue in Fujian and, further south, Nanyue. The Qin and then the Han pushed into the south, and after the Han conquest of Nanyue in 111 BCE the Yue lands became part of China. The Yue are among the ancestors of many peoples of southern China and northern Vietnam.
